title: The effect of Relativistic Aberration on Cosmological Distances

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states: 'Equation 5 clearly doesn't hold if the expansion of the Universe between us and the CO is faster than c, but in that case we simply can't detect any light signal from the CO so the problem doesn't arise.' This is false in standard FLRW cosmology: objects with recession velocities greater than c are routinely observed, e.g. galaxies at z > 1.7, and superluminal recession does not imply an event horizon or nondetection.

The derivation adds an additional (1+z)^(-2) solid-angle factor for relativistic aberration in Eq. (14), leading to d_L = R_0^3/R_1^2 r_1 = R_0(1+z)^2 r_1 instead of the standard FLRW result d_L = R_0(1+z) r_1. The FLRW null-geodesic luminosity-distance formula already includes the effects of relative motion of comoving observers (including aberration), so this is double-counting. In the exactly solvable Milne empty universe, the standard formula matches the special-relativistic result, whereas the proposed formula gives an extra factor of (1+z).

Equation (26) defines dS_O = r_O^2 dOmega_O, but Eq. (28) asserts dS_O = r_O^2(1+z)^2 dOmega_O for the same quantities. Substituting Eqs. (21) and (28) into Eq. (30) gives r_G = r_O(1+z)^2, which together with Eqs. (24) and (29) yields d_L/[d_A(1+z)^2] = 1+z, not 1. Thus the claimed Etherington relation (31) does not follow from the stated equations.

Equation (3) treats x^i as a position vector and writes x_i = g_{ik} x^k, then differentiates it. In general relativity, coordinates are not components of a position vector in curved spacetime, so g_{ik}x^k is not a coordinate-covariant position vector. The covariant velocity is g_{ik} dx^k/dtau, not d(g_{ik}x^k)/dtau.
The paper refers to the 'Volkov-Oppenheimer limit'. The correct name is the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) limit. This is a clear misattribution of the physical limit.

The text compares a solid-angle magnification factor of about 10^6 to CMB temperature anisotropies of order 10^-6 K: 'It's interesting to notice that the effect on the surface area of every point of the CMB is increasing it by 10^6, while the temperature anisotropies of the CMB are in the order of 10^-6 K.' This compares a dimensionless factor with a temperature in kelvin, which is physically meaningless and misleading.

Equation (43) defines I_G := F_nu / dS'_O. That expression has units of flux density per area, not specific intensity (power per area per solid angle per frequency). The definition omits the solid-angle and frequency content needed for surface brightness, so the subsequent specific-intensity relation is dimensionally inconsistent.
